sources.title: United Nations Editorial Manual Online — Spelling (spell_print_3.pdf)
sources.publisher: United Nations, Department for General Assembly and Conference Management (DGACM)
sources.scope: Spelling authority and spelling list for United Nations documents (English). 24 pages; footer "United Nations Editorial Manual Online © 2004–2023 (New York) ... Last updated on 19 September 2023."
sources.evidence: Authority statement (p. 1): "The Concise Oxford English Dictionary, twelfth edition, is the current authority for spelling in the United Nations. If more than one spelling is given in the dictionary, use the form listed first unless otherwise indicated below. The online Oxford Dictionary (https://premium.oxforddictionaries.com/english/) (set to British and World English) is an acceptable alternative."  ||  Notes key (p. 1): "* Indicates a change from previous practice. ** Indicates an exception to the twelfth edition of the Concise Oxford English Dictionary. *** Indicates both a change from previous practice and an exception to the twelfth edition."  ||  List entries for the organize family are printed in -z form, with no -ise variant listed: "organization", "organization chart (not “organigram(me)” or “organizational chart”)", "organize".  ||  Other -ize/-ization entries printed without exception markers: "globalization", "globalize", "minimize", "liberalization", "liberalize", "privatization", "privatize", "specialize", "stabilization", "stabilize", "summarize", "utilize", "digitalize (adapt a system or process)", "digitize (convert material into a digital format)", "de-emphasize", "re-emphasize", "endogenization", "counter-urbanization", "inter-organizational", "Judaize".  ||  -ise entries printed by the same list: "analyse", "catalyse", "paralyse", "practise (verb)" (paired with "practice (noun)").  ||  Requested specific entries, quoted exactly as listed: "adviser"; "colour"; "centre, centred, centring"; "per cent"; "modelled, modelling"; "organization"; "organize".  ||  The bare word "model" does not appear as its own headword (only "modelled, modelling" and inside compounds such as "demographic-economic model"). The string "percent" does not occur anywhere in the 24-page document; only the two-word "per cent" is listed. The bare word "color" does not occur; only "colour" is listed.  ||  No -ize or -ise entry carries an asterisk, so none of them is marked as an exception to the Concise Oxford English Dictionary, twelfth edition.
sources.note: Retrieved with curl using a browser User-Agent; the default curl User-Agent is blocked by CloudFront (HTTP 403 "Request blocked."). PDF text extracted to scratch with pypdf 6.19.0 and audited by grep. The Concise Oxford English Dictionary, 12th edition, itself is proprietary and could not be consulted; the "first-listed form" claim rests on the UN list's own printed entries, which is what the "unless otherwise indicated below" clause applies to.

sources.title: United Nations Editorial Manual Online (DGACM landing page)
sources.publisher: United Nations, Department for General Assembly and Conference Management (DGACM)
sources.scope: Entry point of the current UN Editorial Manual; links the sections (Abbreviations, Capitalization, Numbers/dates/time, Punctuation, Spelling, etc.).
sources.evidence: HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27; page <title> reads "United Nations Editorial Manual Online | Department for General Assembly and Conference Management".  ||  Section URLs verified: /content/editorial-manual/abbreviations, /capitalization, /numbers-dates-time, /italics, /punctuation.
sources.note: This is the working URL for the manual. The URL cited in rules/sources.md and config/profiles/un-v1.json, https://editorial.un.org/, did not resolve from this network on 2026-09-27 (see entry editorial-un-org).

sources.title: United Nations Editorial Manual Online — Numbers, dates and time
sources.scope: Official guidance on numerals, percentages, ranges and dates in UN documents (English).
sources.evidence: Exact note under "Percentages": "Note: Both the percentage sign (%) and “per cent” may be used in running text, as long as the document is internally consistent. The percentage sign should not be used in resolutions."  ||  Range guidance: "When linking two numbers, use the following forms: An en dash (–): A substantial increase in production (12–14 per cent) is expected."  ||  Negative amounts: "There was continued negative growth of 1.9 per cent in 2026."
sources.note: Retrieved by curl with a browser User-Agent; page text extracted with Python. This directly contradicts the paraphrase in rules/sources.md that the manual says "per cent" should normally be written out while % may be used only in tables where space is limited: the live manual permits either form in running text if the document is internally consistent.

sources.title: United Nations Editorial Manual Online — Abbreviations and acronyms
sources.scope: Official guidance on abbreviations, short titles and initialisms in UN documents (English).
sources.evidence: Exact text under "Short titles": "A short title may be used to replace a name or title that occurs many times in a document, provided that the full name is used the first time it occurs and that there is no risk of ambiguity: the Assembly, the Council, the Committee, the United Kingdom, the United States."
sources.note: No statement banning a bare "US" as a country name was found in this section, the Capitalization section or the Spelling list. The full form "the United States" is the name the manual uses; the rule's specific prohibition is not documented by the sections reviewed in this pass.

sources.title: UN Geneva web style guide
sources.scope: Writing style for the English pages of the ungeneva.org website.
sources.evidence: Exact text: "This is the English version of the style guide, and it gives advice exclusively on writing styles on the English pages of the website. In line with the United Nations Editorial Manual, the website uses British English unless otherwise declared. Point of reference is the Oxford English Dictionary."  ||  Exact text: "It builds on existing writing conventions such as the United Nations Editorial Manual or UNTerm while taking into account a web perspective as well as specific vocabulary used at UN Geneva."  ||  The page contains no occurrence of "-ize", "-ise", "organiz", "organis" or any per-word spelling prescription; its only spelling statement is the British-English sentence quoted above.
sources.note: First webfetch attempt timed out; retrieved successfully with curl and a browser User-Agent (HTTP 200). Scope is explicitly limited to ungeneva.org English pages, not to UN documents in general.

sources.title: SDG indicator metadata — 3.1.1 Maternal mortality ratio (Metadata-03-01-01.pdf)
sources.scope: Official indicator metadata defining the maternal mortality ratio and distinguishing it from other maternal mortality measures.
sources.evidence: Exact text: "The maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is defined as the number of maternal deaths during a given time period per 100 000 live births during the same time period. It depicts the risk of maternal death relative to the number of live births and essentially captures (1) above."  ||  Exact text: "By contrast, the maternal mortality rate (MMRate) is calculated as the number of maternal deaths divided by person-years lived by women of reproductive age. The MMRate captures both the risk of maternal death per pregnancy or per total birth (live birth or stillbirth), and the level of fertility in the population."  ||  Exact text: "In addition to the MMR and the MMRate, it is possible to calculate the adult lifetime risk of maternal mortality for women in the population. An alternative measure of maternal mortality, the proportion of deaths among women of reproductive age that are due to maternal causes (PM), is calculated as the number of maternal deaths divided by the total deaths among women aged 15–49 years."
sources.note: Downloaded with curl (HTTP 200) and text extracted with pypdf. This confirms that "maternal mortality rate" is a distinct, defined technical measure in UN metadata, not a misspelling of the ratio.

sources.title: WHO fact sheet — Maternal mortality
sources.scope: Current WHO global maternal mortality figures and indicator naming.
sources.evidence: Key facts: "Between 2000 and 2023, the maternal mortality ratio (MMR, number of maternal deaths per 100 000 live births) dropped by about 40% worldwide."  ||  The fact sheet itself uses the word "rate" once when quoting the SDG target: "reducing the global MMR to less than 70 per 100 000 births, with no country having a maternal mortality rate of more than twice the global average".
sources.note: Retrieved with curl (HTTP 200). Shows both that "ratio" is the WHO indicator name for deaths per 100 000 live births and that "maternal mortality rate" appears even in official UN/WHO prose, so flagging the phrase as an automatic error would be unreliable.

sources.title: United Nations Guidelines for gender-inclusive language in English
sources.scope: UN staff guidance on gender-inclusive English (section 1.2 covers gender-biased expressions).
sources.evidence: Section heading: "1.2 Avoid gender-biased expressions or expressions that reinforce gender stereotypes".  ||  Under "Discriminatory examples:" the list includes: "“Oh, that’s women's work.”"  ||  The section prescribes a general test, not a replacement term: "How do I know if I am using discriminatory language? Reverse the gender: Would reversing the designation or the term from masculine to feminine or vice versa change the mea[ning]..."
sources.note: Page text retrieved with curl (HTTP 200). This is the closest primary UN source found for the phrase, but it lists "women's work" as a stereotype-reinforcing exclamation and never prescribes replacing it with "female labour-force participation rate"; that pair remains unsourced (see entry womens-work-replacement-pair).

sources.title: UN Women — Gender mainstreaming guidance: Guidelines for the use of language as a driver of equality and inclusivity
sources.publisher: UN Women (Regional Office for Europe and Central Asia)
sources.scope: UN Women language guidance for gender-responsive communications (39 pages).
sources.evidence: Exact text using the phrase descriptively: "However, because care work is considered ‘women's work’ it is mostly unpaid; because it is not assigned a monetary value, it is not measured; because it is not visible, it is not taken into account in policymaking."  ||  Its actual avoid/prefer rules are of a different kind: "Avoid the unnecessary references to gender: adding ‘’female’’, ‘’women’’ or ‘’male’’ to generic neutral terms should be avoided." (examples: "Cleaning lady" → "Cleaner", "Male nurse" → "Nurse").
sources.note: Downloaded with curl (HTTP 200) and extracted with pypdf. UN Women's own guidance document uses the phrase "women's work" in running prose, which is evidence against treating the phrase as an institutional error.

sources.title: Disability-Inclusive Language Guidelines (United Nations Office at Geneva)
sources.scope: UNOG guidance implementing the UN Disability Inclusion Strategy (2019); oral and written communications (11 pages).
sources.evidence: Annex table columns: "Recommended language | Language to be avoided"; the recommended row reads "persons with disabilities / people with disabilities (only in Easy Read documents, informal text and oral speech)" and the avoid cell reads "disabled person, handicapped, person with special needs, handicapable, atypical, person living with a disability, differently abled, people of all abilities, people of determination".  ||  "handicapped" also appears in the avoid cell for physical disability: "crippled, invalid, deformed, lame, handicapped, physically challenged, person with physical limitations, limp" (recommended: "person with a physical disability").  ||  General principle: "1. USE PEOPLE-FIRST LANGUAGE People-first language is the most widely accepted language for referring to persons with disabilities. It is also the language used in the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities."
sources.note: Downloaded with curl (HTTP 200) and text extracted with pypdf. Direct support for the profile pair "handicapped" → "persons with disabilities".

sources.title: United Nations Disability-Inclusive Communications Guidelines
sources.publisher: United Nations, Department of Global Communications
sources.scope: System-wide guidance on inclusive and accessible UN communications.
sources.evidence: Index description (from https://www.un.org/en/disabilitystrategy/resources, HTTP 200): "The Guidelines provide practical information on how to include and represent persons with disabilities in communications, and how to make UN communications inclusive of and accessible to persons with disabilities."  ||  UN Digital Library record exists (record 4042358, PDF file 1401388-EN.pdf).
sources.note: The digitallibrary.un.org record returned HTTP 202 (bot challenge) to automated fetch on 2026-09-27, so the full text was not downloaded in this pass; the companion UN Geneva language guidelines (previous entry) carry the quotable terminology table. Directory page https://www.un.org/en/disabilitystrategy/resources returned 200.

sources.title: Rabat Plan of Action on the prohibition of advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred (A/HRC/22/17/Add.4)
sources.publisher: United Nations Human Rights Council / OHCHR
sources.scope: Official UN document symbol A/HRC/22/17/Add.4, adopted by experts at Rabat, Morocco, 5 October 2012; contains the six-part threshold test used for incitement analysis.
sources.evidence: Document identity: "Conclusions and recommendations emanating from the four regional expert workshops organized by OHCHR in 2011, and adopted by experts at the meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on 5 October 2012 ... United Nations A/HRC/22/17/Add.4".  ||  Six-part test: "In this regard, a six-part threshold test was proposed for expressions considered as criminal offences: (a) Context: ... Analysis of the context should place the speech act within the social and political context prevalent at the time the speech was made and disseminated; (b) Speaker: The speaker's position or status in the society should be considered, specifically the individual's or organization's standing in the context of the audience to whom the speech is directed; (c) Intent: Article 20 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights anticipates intent. Negligence and recklessness are not sufficient ... (d) Content and form ... (e) Extent of the speech act ..."  ||  Symbol URL https://docs.un.org/A/HRC/22/17/Add.4 returned HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27.
sources.note: Text extracted from the OHCHR-hosted English PDF https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Issues/Opinion/SeminarRabat/Rabat_draft_outcome.pdf (HTTP 200; pages carry "A/HRC/22/17/Add.4" and "GE.13-10151"). The UN Digital Library file https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/746343/files/A_HRC_22_17_Add.4-EN.pdf returned HTTP 202 (bot challenge) and the OHCHR HTML landing page /en/documents/outcome-documents/rabat-plan-action returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; both exist per search index.

sources.title: UN hate speech portal (Say #NoToHate)
sources.publisher: United Nations, Department of Global Communications
sources.scope: UN-wide hate speech hub: definitions, prevention, resources.
sources.evidence: HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27. Page hosts the "UN Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech" section and links "Understanding hate speech", "International human rights law" and "Key human rights instruments".
sources.note: Confirms the cite string "un.org/en/hate-speech" used by lib/rules-hs.mjs resolves.

sources.title: What is hate speech? (UN hate speech portal)
sources.publisher: United Nations, Department of Global Communications
sources.scope: UN definition of hate speech used by the rules' knowledge base.
sources.evidence: Exact quote: "the UN Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech defines hate speech as… ‘any kind of communication in speech, writing or behaviour, that attacks or uses pejorative or discriminatory language with reference to a person or a group on the basis of who they are, in other words, based on their religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor.’"  ||  Exact caveat: "However, to date there is no universal definition of hate speech under international human rights law."
sources.note: HTTP 200; matches the citation string embedded in lib/rules-hs.mjs for UE-HS001.

sources.title: United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech
sources.scope: UN-wide strategy adopted 18 June 2019; foundation of the hate-speech rule family.
sources.evidence: Landing text: "UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech on 18 June 2019. This first UN-wide initiative designed to tackle hate speech provides a road map on how the Organization can support and complement States' efforts."  ||  Full PDF (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/action_plan_on_hate_speech_en.pdf) returned HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27.
sources.note: Both the section URL and the PDF resolve; the strategy cites the Rabat Plan of Action as related framework.

sources.title: UNTERM — United Nations Multilingual Terminology Database
sources.scope: Official UN terminology in the six official languages; used for approved designations (e.g. "Taiwan, province of China", "the question of Jammu and Kashmir").
sources.evidence: HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27 (redirects to https://unterm.un.org/unterm2/).  ||  About page (https://unterm.un.org/unterm2/about): "UNTERM is the official global terminology portal of the United Nations. It provides terminology and nomenclature in subjects relevant to the work of the United Nations."  ||  The UN Geneva web style guide itself links its "Related info: ... UNTERM" to href="https://unterm.un.org/unterm2/en/".
sources.note: The bare domain unterm.org does NOT serve the UN database: on 2026-09-27 plain http://unterm.org/ returned an unrelated German site (base href http://www.unterm-durchschnitt.de/, title "Start. Unterm Durchschnitt") and https://unterm.org/ failed the TLS handshake (SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL) from this network. Use unterm.un.org.

sources.title: UNESCO UIS / SDG 4 indicator metadata — completion rate (4.1.2) and lower secondary completion rate
sources.scope: Official names and definitions of education completion-rate indicators.
sources.evidence: UIS SDG 4 indicator list (HTTP 200): "4.1.2 Completion rate (primary education, lower secondary education, upper secondary education)".  ||  SDG 4.1.2 metadata definition: "Percentage of a cohort of children or young people aged 3-5 years above the intended age for the last grade of each level of education who have completed that grade."  ||  World Bank/UIS series glossary (SE.SEC.CMPT.LO.ZS): "Lower secondary education completion rate is measured as the gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education (general and pre-vocational)."
sources.note: The official indicator name is "lower secondary completion rate" (World Bank/UIS series name) or "Completion rate (… lower secondary …)" (UIS SDG list); the README form "lower-secondary completion rate" matches the official term apart from hyphenation. The UIS glossary entry (https://databrowser.uis.unesco.org/resources/glossary/3201) and the SDG metadata mirror (https://worldbank.github.io/sdg-metadata/phase-2/metadata/en/4-1-2) were reachable on 2026-09-27.

sources.title: IEA — Energy and AI, Executive summary (data centre electricity demand)
sources.scope: Primary statistics for data centre electricity consumption and its share of demand.
sources.evidence: Exact quote: "Data centres accounted for around 1.5% of the world's electricity consumption in 2024, or 415 terawatt-hours (TWh)."  ||  Exact quote: "Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030."  ||  Projection wording: "global electricity consumption for data centres is projected to double to reach around 945 TWh by 2030 in the Base Case, representing just under 3% of total global electricity consumption in 2030" (Energy and AI, Energy demand from AI chapter).
sources.note: HTTP 200 on 2026-09-27. IEA is not a UN body; it is the primary source for this statistic and no UN body defines it. IEA usage is "data centres" (British spelling) and "share of … electricity consumption/demand"; the README phrase "data centres' share of electricity demand" is consistent with IEA wording.

sources.title: No source found — replacement pair "women's work" → "female labour-force participation rate"
sources.scope: Claim check for the UE-TE002 pair carried in config/profiles/un-v1.json.
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE. No primary UN source was found that prescribes replacing "women's work" or "female work" with "female labour-force participation rate". Checked on 2026-09-27: UN Guidelines for gender-inclusive language in English (lists "Oh, that's women's work." only as a stereotype-reinforcing discriminatory example, with no replacement term), UN Women gender-mainstreaming language guidance (uses the phrase "women's work" descriptively), UN Geneva web style guide, UN Editorial Manual Spelling list, and web searches across un.org/unwomen.org/ilo.org. The URL shown is the closest source reviewed. The pair as configured is unsourced.

sources.title: Concise Oxford English Dictionary, 12th edition (spelling authority, proprietary)
sources.scope: The dictionary named as the current UN spelling authority.
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE. The dictionary text could not be retrieved (proprietary; no licensed copy in this environment; the OUP product URL returned an HTTP 202 bot challenge). The authority claim itself is verified from the UN manual quote, but the "first-listed form" for any given word could not be checked against the dictionary directly; the UN spelling list's printed entries were used instead.

sources.title: editorial.un.org — manual URL cited by the repo (unresolved)
sources.scope: URL cited as the UN Editorial Manual Online in rules/sources.md and config/profiles/un-v1.json.
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE. Did not resolve from this network on 2026-09-27: https://editorial.un.org/, http://editorial.un.org/ and https://www.editorial.un.org/ all failed (curl exit code 35/000, connection could not be established). The manual's live home is https://www.un.org/dgacm/en/content/editorial-manual (see entry un-editorial-manual-landing). Repo citations pointing at editorial.un.org should be repointed.

sources.title: OHCHR — The Rabat Plan of Action (outcome document landing page)
sources.scope: OHCHR landing page for the Rabat Plan of Action with language versions.
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE (retrieval only). The page exists (indexed content confirms "The Rabat Plan of Action was adopted by experts at the wrap-up meeting in Rabat on 4-5 October 2012") but returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch on 2026-09-27. Use https://docs.un.org/A/HRC/22/17/Add.4 as the canonical citation instead.

sources.title: The Guardian and Observer style guide — Z entry (-ze endings)
sources.scope: Generic British -ise spelling for the generic-british-english profile. Not a United Nations source: it exists so a UN document can adopt external British house style when a publisher requires it.
sources.evidence: Entry "-ze endings", quoted exactly: "use -se, even if this upsets your (American) spellchecker, eg emphasise, realise; but capsize".
sources.note: Retrieved 27 September 2026 as HTML. The guide is a newsroom house style, not a UN authority; the profile source field says so explicitly.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (A/RES/61/106)
sources.scope: Basis for refusing demeaning and pity-framed descriptions of persons with disabilities (UE-DM001); the sex-or-gender branch additionally cites the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW, 1979) inside lib/rules-hs.mjs.
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE (retrieval only): no live fetch was performed for this entry on 2026-09-28 — verify that the URL resolves before release. The CRPD was adopted by General Assembly resolution A/RES/61/106 on 13 December 2006.

sources.title: United Nations Member States — official list of current member-country designations
sources.scope: The United Nations forms of member-country names used by the country-name terminology pairs (UE-TE005). Growth of the pair set beyond the nine recorded in the profile requires a re-check of this page or of UNTERM records.
sources.evidence: Page fetched 2026-10-01; the list entries for the relevant members read exactly: "Myanmar", "Türkiye", "Eswatini", "Cabo Verde", "North Macedonia", "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)", "Côte D'Ivoire", "Timor-Leste", "Democratic Republic of the Congo".  ||  The page title reads "Member States" under un.org/en/about-us.
sources.note: The profile pairs map the superseded forms (Burma, Turkey, Swaziland, Cape Verde, Macedonia, Holland, Ivory Coast, East Timor, Zaire) to these current designations. Historical and common-name contexts remain legitimate in prose outside United Nations editorial stance; the rule asks for the current form in UN copy and the pair is allowlistable per project.

sources.title: Global Migration Group Statement on the Human Rights of Migrants in Irregular Situation and OHCHR guidance on the economic, social and cultural rights of migrants in an irregular situation
sources.scope: Basis for the migration terminology pairs under UE-TE002: the United Nations frames migration status as an administrative condition, and the established form is "migrants in an irregular situation".
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE (retrieval only): OHCHR returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch on 2026-10-01, as it did for the Rabat Plan entry above. The phrase "migrants in an irregular situation" is used throughout the OHCHR publication named in the title, the 2010 Global Migration Group statement of the same subject, and Global Compact for Migration materials (A/RES/73/195); verify a quotable line before relying on this entry in an institutional audit.

sources.title: United Nations development usage — "developing countries" and "developing economies" as the standard designations
sources.publisher: United Nations (DESA, per current development statistics usage)
sources.scope: Basis for the "Third World" pair under UE-TE002: current United Nations development writing designates "developing countries" or "developing economies", not the Cold-War-era "Third World".
sources.note: HONEST NEGATIVE (retrieval only): no single UN style rule banning "Third World" was retrieved on 2026-10-01. The pair rests on standing UN development-statistics usage (UN DESA designations) rather than on a quoted prohibition — verify against the current Editorial Manual before an institutional audit relies on it.
